summary: Records a bounded history of a store's state so it can be undone, redone or stepped through, and reports what it cannot fully restore.
description: Watches a store and records an entry per commit, keeping `entries[currentIndex]` always equal to live state. History is bounded by `maxHistory` (default 50): the oldest entry is dropped first, never the current one, and lowering the bound while you are mid-travel drops the redo tail instead. A new write truncates the redo stack, as undo/redo everywhere does. An undo is an ordinary store commit — every other subscriber sees it as a normal change, not a special replay — so nothing in the graph needs to know time travel exists. Where it is honest rather than magical: values that can only be captured by reference (Models, Collections, functions, cyclic objects) are *not* deep-copied, so undoing does not restore their internal state. `fullyRestorable` and `byReferenceKeys` say exactly which keys those are, rather than letting the feature quietly under-deliver. Coalescing (`coalesceMs`, off by default) folds rapid same-key writes into one entry so undo steps match user intent instead of keystrokes — and never folds into the entry a navigation just landed on, which would destroy the state you had just undone to.
whenToUse: Undo/redo over shared state — a form, an editor, a builder, a drawing surface — and stepping back through state while debugging. Place one per store you want tracked; wire the Undo / Redo node to the buttons. For a single named checkpoint rather than a moving history, use State Snapshot. Check `fullyRestorable` before advertising undo over state that holds Collections or Models.

ports.storeName: The store to track. Tracking is reference-counted, so a second State History node on the same store does not wipe the first one's history.
ports.trackKeys: Comma-separated keys to track; empty tracks the whole store. Only tracked keys are restored, so a filtered history leaves everything else alone.
ports.maxHistory: Entries kept, default 50, floor 2. This is a memory bound: an unbounded history in a long-running app grows without limit.
ports.coalesceMs: Window in which consecutive writes to the same keys fold into one entry. 0 (default) records every commit separately. Set it to roughly a typing pause when undo should step by word rather than by character.
ports.enabled: False pauses recording without discarding history. Resuming records an entry if state drifted while paused, so the history never claims a change did not happen.
ports.clearHistory: Discards every entry and starts again from live state.
ports.done: Signal; the history was thrown away and re-baselined.
ports.unchanged: Signal; there was nothing to throw away, because the history was already just its baseline.
ports.completed: Signal; fires after either outcome. There is no Failure port — this node is the tracker for its own store name, so there is no store it can be asked for and fail to find.
ports.currentIndex: Where in the history live state sits. Not at the end means you are mid-travel and a new write will truncate the redo tail.
ports.canUndo: Whether an earlier entry exists — wire it to the Undo button's enabled state rather than guessing.
ports.fullyRestorable: False when any tracked key in the history could only be captured by reference, so undo cannot fully restore it.
ports.byReferenceKeys: Which keys those are. Show this rather than letting an author believe undo is total.
ports.history: Entry descriptors (not the states themselves) for building a timeline UI, each flagged with whether it is partial.
ports.historyChanged: Fires when an entry is added, dropped, or the current position moves.

patterns: `canUndo`/`canRedo` → the buttons' enabled state, so the affordance matches reality.
`coalesceMs` around 300–500 for text input, so an undo removes a word rather than a letter.
`history` → a Repeater for a visible timeline, with `currentIndex` marking where you are.
Surface `byReferenceKeys` in a developer-facing view when the store holds Collections, instead of discovering the limit through a confusing undo.
antiPatterns: Leaving `maxHistory` unbounded-by-intent in a long-running app: every entry is retained state.
Assuming undo restores everything. A key listed in `byReferenceKeys` shares its object with the entry, so its internal state was never copied.
Tracking the whole store when only a form's keys need undoing — unrelated writes then become undo steps the user did not make.
